title: BIAS-ID: A Framework for Analyzing Transformation Biases in AI-Generated Image Detectors
claim: Training on differently processed real and fake images makes detectors rely on processing artifacts, producing biased predictions that depend on test-time compression.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right, each a score/shift line plot beside an accuracy heatmap
description: A single-row figure with three sub-figures, (a) to (c). Each has two stacked line plots on the left and a blue heatmap on the right. The top line plot shows the mean detector score for real images (red circles) and fake images (blue crosses) against JPEG quality, from uncompressed down to 10. Below it, a mean score shift (MSS) plot shows the change relative to the uncompressed score. The heatmap shows accuracy for combinations of real and fake JPEG quality, with a color bar from 0 to 1. In (a), trained with JPEG augmentation, scores are stable and the heatmap is uniformly dark, meaning high accuracy. In (b), trained on compressed real and uncompressed fake images, scores collapse and accuracy is high only for uncompressed fakes. In (c), trained on uncompressed real and compressed fake images, accuracy is high only in the uncompressed-real row. Captions below describe each training setup.
caption: Demonstration of how training detectors on differently processed real and fake images can cause biased predictions. For each detector (a)-(c), the plot on the left shows the mean scores and mean score shifts (MSSs) for real ( ) and fake ( ) images, with 95% CIs depicted as shaded bands (very narrow, best viewed when zoomed in). The heatmap on the right depicts the detector’s accuracy (assuming a decision threshold of 0.5) when tested on different combinations of real and fake quality levels.
abstract: Given the surge of harmful AI-generated imagery online, reliably distinguishing authentic images from generated ones has become an urgent research topic. While many proposed detection methods demonstrate high accuracy in controlled settings, their performance often degrades substantially when tested on real-world data. A potential root cause is subtle bias in the detectors' training data. As a result, detectors may rely on spurious correlations instead of learning true forensic artifacts. While recent studies have identified this problem and developed countermeasures, there is not yet an established protocol to evaluate how biased a detector actually is. In this work, we therefore take a step back: First, we discuss what it means for a detector to be biased, and how this differs from a lack of robustness. Second, we propose BIAS-ID, a transparent framework for analyzing and quantifying the presence of transformation biases in AI-generated image detectors. We validate our framework by evaluating six detectors across two datasets, revealing that several state-of-the-art detection methods are strongly affected by common, processing-related biases. Our results highlight the importance of bias-aware evaluation for developing reliable AI-generated image detectors. We provide an easy-to-use library and code to reproduce our results at https://github.com/jonasricker/biasid.
